summary: A satirical news-style piece about a fictional 'Toxic Fog' that engulfed a continent starting September 18, 2023 in New New Amsterdam. It mocks the supposed upsides, including a greenhouse stock boom, breathing-gadget fashion, fog-inspired art, dramatic weather reporting and 'foggers' parties, while ending with a reminder that it is satire about air pollution warnings.
one_line: Satirical article lampooning a fictional continent-wide toxic fog and the odd social, economic, technological and artistic booms it supposedly spawned.
key_facts: Toxic Fog first appeared on September 18, 2023, when residents of New New Amsterdam woke to an eerie, pallid mist.
The fog was initially mistaken for an early onset of winter fog before being identified as Toxic Fog.
Dr. Astra Lungs, described as a world-renowned respiratory expert, coined the term and joked, "Breathing was honestly becoming mundane."
The fog spread across urban and rural areas and international borders, and is called 'the great equalizer in gaseous form'.
Local introvert Bob Hermit welcomed the fog as an excuse to avoid sun exposure and social gatherings without judgment.
The greenhouse industry got a windfall as air-filtering plants became a 'new gold rush', with greenhouses called the 'Iron Lungs of the modern age'.
Stock prices of companies like PureO2Flora skyrocketed.
Economists dubbed the effect of the 1% inhaling the same air as everyone else 'The Great Equilibration'.
The must-have fashion accessory of 2024 was the deluxe personal breathing apparatus, not a smartwatch or smartphone.
Technology guru Gina Gismo praised her FogBeGone® headpiece, saying she can last days in the fog and that its LED display doesn't hurt.
Monochrome canvas works depicting the fog exploded in sales, and Sid Bleak's 'Eternal Monochrome Mornings' sold for over six figures at auction.
Celebrity weatherman Chuck Cyclone said forecasts have become an avant-garde genre: part thriller, part horror, with comedy and improv.
New social customs include respirator tipping, filter fashion statements, and underground parties called 'foggers'.
The article closes by stating it is satire about long-standing predictions on air pollution, and urges readers to check their breathing apparatus and plant stocks.
